utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. We are starting our hearing. Registrar, kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. Today we are Wednesday, the 19th of March, 2008. I would like to greet all the representatives of the Prosecution, Mr. Seselj, as well as all the people assisting us. Amongst other people, the interpreters, who are doing a very valuable job. So today we need to resume with the cross-examination of the witness. I shall therefore give the floor to Mr. Seselj, who will have an hour and a half for his cross-examination of the witness. And, Witness, of course I would also like to greet you, and I am sure that your testimony will be finished today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cakalic, you have testified in three trials in The Hague, Slavko Dokmanovic, Slobodan Milosevic, and the third trial Mrksic Jovan; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You testified in open session, publicly under your own name and surname?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what about this particular trial? Did you ask to have protective measures under a pseudonym and testify in private session?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never asked for that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down and pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So the Prosecution treated you here as a secret witness; right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think Your Honours that this is a very important issue, and it's not the first time that the Prosecution asked for protective measures without the witness having requested it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, did you think there was some danger to you in coming in here to testify against me?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Any danger from me or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Again, we have to observe a pause between questions and answers. I'm sorry, because if you do not do that then we will not be able to understand anything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As I was saying, you consider that there's no threat to you from me or from my friends or my political party; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you're testifying in a very relaxed fashion, is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cakalic, that was important for me to hear that from you personally. Now I consider that you told the truth about everything that happened to you, so I can accept your statement almost entirely. So as far as you're concerned I'm going to deal with some issues that are secondary as far as you are concerned, but they can be important for me. I hope you understand that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said here -- rather, you were talking about how you were arrested in the Vukovar Hospital and the fact that after that you were taken in buses to the Vukovar barracks. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And while you were still in the buses some people gathered together whom you called Chetniks and they threatened that they would kill you all. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you saw that they were Chetniks of Montenegrin ethnicity because they wore the traditional Montenegrin caps did they not?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now after that when these Chetniks left for a time you left the bus, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the barracks. Now, you said in testifying at the Milosevic trial that after you heard -- left the buses that military policemen turned up who started to beat the people; right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And among those military policemen who beat the prisoners in the JNA barracks, you recognised some Muslims among them. There were several Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't seem to remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you say that in the Slobodan Milosevic trial and the transcript of it, and it is record on page 9 or 10 of the transcript. And since the transcript was provided to me from a book, not directly, it wasn't directly translated from the original, I don't know what page it is, but I'm sure the Prosecution were able to find the reference. Anyway, Richard May was surprised to hear that and asked you to explain, and you did indeed explain and confirmed that there were Muslims there. Of course there were Serbs, too, but that there were several Muslims who beat the prisoners, swore at them, and so on. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I just want you to confirm that. Now, in that same trial, the Slobodan Milosevic trial, you spoke about the people who beat you at Ovcara, and you said that they were Vukovar Chetniks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were those and other people I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There were JNA soldiers, people you couldn't recognise and didn't know, but you did recognise many as being local Vukovar inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know the local Vukovar people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You referred to them as Chetniks, did you not?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't call them Chetniks, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you say here in the Slobodan Milosevic trial transcript that -- you say that expressly. You say that they were Chetniks from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't deny that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now tell me, how do you differentiate between Chetniks and JNA soldiers? How can you distinguish between the two? Well, the soldier of the Yugoslav People's Army were soldiers who had taken the oath; right? Isn't that right? Did you take the oath when you were in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm an invalid so I didn't serve in the JNA, so I don't know a lot about the army. But if you took the oath when you joined up, and I do believe you did, then probably you would act upon the oath you took and respect it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In way do you mean fulfil the oath?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know what the text of the actual oath was? I'll try and interpret it so you can deny it or accept it. As soldiers we would take an oath and pledge that we would defend the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yugoslavia and the constitutional order. That was the oath the soldiers took, all of them.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you can confirm that can you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So when the territorial sovereignty of the country was jeopardised and the territorial integrity and sovereignty and constitutional order, it was our duty to defend the state and the constitutional system; right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Right. We agree there on that point. Now, I'm interested in this difference. You said that there were JNA soldiers and there were Chetniks. Now, were you able to come to that conclusion by some outward appearance?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they said they were Chetniks themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the Yugoslav People's Army soldiers were wearing their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, but the Chetniks also very frequently had JNA uniforms on.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: For example the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, do you know that they had their volunteers there too; for example, they were given uniforms -- issued uniforms, in Bubanj Potok barracks in Belgrade, and they all wore JNA uniforms just took the five-pointed star off?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you noticed that some soldiers had the five-pointed star insignia and others didn't, and those who didn't had different insignia or badges or cockades as they were called, but they weren't all the same were they?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There were a lot of different badges and insignia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you Mr. Cakalic. Now, you said on several occasions that among the officers who were at Ovcara that you were there when some were beating people or some issued orders for others to beat, and you mentioned somebody with a whistle in his hand and when he gave the signal group, the groups of people that were doing the beating rotated?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said you knew Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: However when the Prosecution showed you a photograph of Colonel Mrksic you were not able to recognise him. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not a sin on my part. A lot of time has gone by.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I understand you completely I'm not -- I don't think you have any sins here in this regard, but I'm just asking you this first question so I can follow on with another question. And the Prosecution towards the end of your testimony at the very end in the Slobodan Milosevic trial informed the Trial Chamber that during your proofing sessions for testimony they showed you a series of photographs and you were not able to recognise Mrksic on those photographs. The Prosecutor said that in court. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, you did mention afterwards, later on when you were in the Sremska Mitrovica prisoner camp where part of the prison was turned into a prisoner camp, you mentioned some Colonel Branko who was the main investigator there; do you remember that? Colonel Branko, according to your statement here, according to your testimony.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did he have a surname?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No. That was a pseudonym. Colonel Branko was in fact a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You can't remember. Right. What I wanted to ask you is whether you saw this Colonel Branko person at Ovcara. That's what I wanted to ask you, but if you don't remember him I'm not going to insist upon the point. I understand your state of health and in view of your years I'm not going to force you to remember if you can't remember, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, we're going to refer now to a number of your previous testimonies in the various trials. Now, you testified in a Belgrade trial against persons accused for crimes committed at Ovcara; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Croats. Yes, from Ovcara. They were taken from Ovcara to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, listen to me carefully. In Belgrade people were accused and the Prosecutor claimed that they personally committed the crime at Ovcara. It's a rather large group of people.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They were all Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The accused?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes and in Belgrade I testified against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's what I wanted you to confirm. Right. And over there you mentioned on page 13 of the transcript of those proceedings, otherwise that was on the 25th of October, 2004, on page 13, you also mentioned Muslims in the barracks, Muslims who seized your valuables, chains, rings, and so on, saying that they would keep it in safekeeping and then return them to you one day. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then on page 20 of the transcript from the Belgrade trial, in testifying about the events in Velepromet, saying that the Vukovar Fakin or guys, young guys, knew that you would arrive, and there were some ten of them there all wearing JNA uniforms and helmets. And then they recognised you, and they said, "Give me Berghofer. Give me Cakalic," and so on, these ruffians?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They said, "So that we can kill them."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So when you say Fakin these are hooligans or ruffians, this term you used, Fakin?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember using that exact term. I don't usually use the word. But anyway -- perhaps I said it in some different way, I don't think I used the word Fakin .

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it's on page 20 from the Belgrade trial and the Trial Chamber can look that up. But the point I want to make is this: They recognised you by your name and they threatened you, and you confirm that, do you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, during that trial you said, and that is to be found on page 32, that at Ovcara among the people who beat you, who was in this cordon, there were soldiers there, but there were also people wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said that then and you now confirm it, do you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Specifically Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, as for Slavko Dokmanovic, you said he was wearing a blue army uniform. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, I do. I remember that. But when you mentioned these people, I am mentioning him first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But he wasn't wearing civilian clothes. He was wearing a blue uniform.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a blue uniform. Well, I can't remember exactly so don't hold me to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That blue uniform could have been either a police uniform or an air force uniform; right? Because in the JNA it was only the air defence and air force that wore blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't pay attention to these details, these minor points that much, because all of us there were fighting to get out of Ovcara. Everybody there sought ways and means to do that, because we felt what was going to happen to us. We had a presentment of what was going to happen. And at Ovcara you know more than 200 people were killed and five or six of us or seven of us were saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Here you stated in several places, Mr. Cakalic, that a total of 207 of you were brought to Ovcara and then 7 were saved. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it strange to you that precisely 200 were killed and out of 207 precisely 7 were saved?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I thought that was a coincidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Doesn't it look as if some cold-blooded criminal mind in a position of power issued the order shoot 200 prisoners, and those who carried out the execution drew up a list, counted off 200, and said, "We will save seven because the orders were to shoot 200"? Did that cross your mind?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never thought about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, now that I'm putting this idea to you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Evidently --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Sorry. This is a kind of speculation. The witness is not able to do this. The accused should put questions and not speculations to the witness. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who said that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Vasiljevic, the chief of the military security service of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This witness doesn't know that, but this witness knows other things and I'm questioning him about other things. So I think that the Prosecutor's objection is not in good order. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, more than once in various trials you were asked who the volunteers were or as you in Croatia say latterly, Dragovoljci, another word for volunteers, and you said that these were people who were going to war voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There were volunteers on both side, were there not?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the Croatian side too?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There were volunteers from various places in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: At the trial in Belgrade, you said that apart from Djapic's party, I think it was Praga's party at the time, though, it's the Croatian Party of Rights; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And Praga was its president at the time?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They had their own paramilitary formation, HOS, the Croatian armed forces; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On page 38 of the transcript from the Belgrade trial you said that all the other parties sent their people to defend Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not parties but people from different towns, different places and villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, yes, you did say that, it's in the transcript, too, but then on page 38, and the Trial Chamber can see that if the transcript is put on the ELMO, Djapic's party, it -- and then all the other parties, too, sent their people to defend Vukovar. "They were all volunteers. Not a single one was forced to do this." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I was a volunteer too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you were a volunteer too. Thank you, sir. Thank you, Mr. Cakalic. Then there's your testimony in the Mrksic case, Mrksic, Sljvancanin, and Radic, and this was on the 13th and 14th of March, 2006; right? It was only two years ago.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And there you also stated, and that's on 5905, that's the page of the transcript, that the Vukovar territorials beat up the prisoners in Ovcara, some with batons, some with weapons, some with fists.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that, and it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't doubt it, Mr. Cakalic. I don't think you're a person who has come here to lie, we were on opposing sides of this war. We fought one against the other, but I do not think you are a man who has come here to lie, and I want you to know that right away. You also confirmed this number of 207 prisoners in total, seven of whom were saved, you, Berghofer, and some others.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They simply selected you out of that large group of 207; right? One person recognised you and he approached you and said he would save you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Another one recognised Berghofer?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you were selected according to different criteria because they felt they had to save you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You did a favour to one of them once and he remembered it?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, maybe somebody else thought that Berghofer didn't deserve to be shot and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So they did use certain criteria according to which they pulled you out of the group?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And there were people within that group who were simply seething with hatred; right? For example, the one called Veliki Boljer, it's as if everybody hated him; right? Everybody was focused on him?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was trampled to death.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. Now, it's not very well that this happened, but I agree with your reply. You mentioned this song here oh, Slobodan send some salad we are about to eat. We shall slaughter Croats and there will be meat. You said the group of about 15 were singing this?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you ever hear this song sung before the war?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were you ever a football fan?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you go to matches? Who did you root for?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dinamo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you go to matches?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did while I lived in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, do you remember in 1990, not long after Tudjman won the elections, there was a big fight and there were disturbances in Zagreb because of a clash between the supports of Crvena Zvezda and Dinamo?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this happened often.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, but that was the worst clash as far as I remember. I'm not a football club supporter but I remember that.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not very fervent either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But there were many people injured in Zagreb on at that day?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you remember at that football match the support of Zvezda sang this song: "Slobodan send some salad, we're about to eat. We shall slaughter Croats and there will be meat." And then the supporters of Dinamo retorted by singing, "Kill the Serb, kill the Serb." Have you ever heard this song?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Didn't you hear about the riots in Zagreb in 1990 and the clashes, the major clashes, a year before the war? You don't remember that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. I won't insist if you don't remember. You made a statement to some Canadian policeman. There was a woman here, a Lieutenant Colonel Kim Carter; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well the OTP evidently didn't feel it necessary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Seselj. Please go more slowly. On line 2, page 15, we have markings here which indicate that a part of the sentence has not been recorded. So please try to slow down. Witness, now, in the wake of the questions that have been put to you, this song that was chanted Slobo, you seem to be demonstrating that this chant -- that these were songs that were chanted by supporters of a football team, and here an incident is quoted, a famous incident that occurred in 1990 in Zagreb during a football match. Can you confirm that what the people were singing in the streets of Vukovar could be the same song that was sung on other occasion in stadiums?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There have always been different football supporters at stadiums everywhere. One side rooted for one side, another for another. It was always the matches between the Red Star from Belgrade and Dinamo from Zagreb that were the most fiery, and with some other clubs, but I never saw any particular evil in that because there may have been people who came to blows, but that was minor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You yourself, did you go to any football matches that pitched the Dinamo of Zagreb against the Red Star of Belgrade? Were you yourself in the stadium? And did you ever hear this kind of song at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stopped going to football matches very early on because I didn't like the football supporters. Some people supported their teams in one way, others in another, and I simply stopped attending football matches. I preferred to watch on television at home. I have not been to a football match for at least 20 years, but I do watch football on television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Cakalic, that you made the statement to the Canadian officers?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you made a statement, and you confirmed this in the Mrksic -- or, rather, in the Mrksic, Sljvancanin, Radic case on transcript page 5939. Some Canadian officers interviewed you, and you gave them that statement. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. I won't insist if you don't.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the Milosevic trial you testified on the 16th of July, 2003; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And six day before that you lived in Kastel Luksic near Split for a while. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the 10th of July, some people from the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia came to see you, from the security service, some sort of secret police, to discuss your testimony in the Milosevic case. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did testify against Milosevic, but I don't remember any policeman coming to see me or asking me to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said that in your testimony in the Mrksic, Sljvancanin, and Radic case on page 5939 of the transcript. Can that page of the transcript be shown on the screen if the registry can do that? 5939. First we can see 5938 to see the last few lines of that page, and then 5939. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You need a little time. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In that same testimony you said that the Serbian people in Vukovar felt under threat just before the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody did. Everybody. Both the Serbs and the Croats and everybody else who lived in Vukovar, all the other nations and ethnicities. You know that Vukovar is a town which had the greatest number of ethnic groups on the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. We'll discuss this at greater length when we round off this topic, the transcripts of the previous trials, once we see this on the screen. In this trial, the trial of Mrksic, Sljvancanin, and Radic, and we can see this on page 6059 of the transcript, when the Prosecutor asked you something about the soldiers who were at Ovcara, you said some of them were in civilian clothes, some had assorted clothing on. For example, the top would be military and the bottom civilian or vice versa.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: "These were the paramilitaries of Vukovar, lads I knew. One of them, for example, approached me when we were already close to the hangar. He asked me, 'Uncle Emil, what are you doing here?'" And so on and so forth. You confirm saying that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall making a statement in the centre for human rights in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what was that statement about?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was it about these events in Vukovar, what you experienced?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume so, but I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, as we don't have that statement, we'll probably never learn. Did you tell the OTP that you had made that statement?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you found this, please, these pages of the transcript? Not yet? I hope you will. And I'll put this aside until you do. You mentioned the fact that among these soldiers at Ovcara there was a man you first said was called Milan Bulic, and then you said his name was Milos Bulic, and you said that he hit you with a metal rod or something like that.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I still have -- I still bear the consequences of that. One of my neck vertebrae is broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mentioned a major who you said was called Milan Lukic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lukic? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And later on he was in charge of the transport from Vukovar to Sremska Mitrovica. You said that he wanted to use an electric baton, to beat prisoners with an electric baton. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that it happened or that you said that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did happen. It happened in a village called Negoslavci. That's where it happened. They were taking us to Belgrade or to Sremska Mitrovica. No, it was Sremska Mitrovica. And the closer we came to Sremska Mitrovica, the less beating there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But later on there was beating in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: A lot?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And it was the military police who did that there; right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was the military police, but there were also military uniforms there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. All right. We'll have an opportunity to talk to those people who were in charge of the beatings in Sremska Mitrovica. The OTP will give us the pleasure of seeing them in the courtroom so we can move on to other matters. Can you describe this electric baton or rod? What does it look like?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a piece of metal, and it has some sort of electromagnetic oscillations probably, and they were used at certain points in time at the demand of the person carrying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Cakalic. I have a statement of yours here, your most recent statement. It was made on the 16th of May, 1992. Police administration, Vukovar. It was the police administration in Vukovar that took your statement, but it was taken somewhere else; right? Was it taken in Zagreb? Where was the Croatian police administration of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It was in Vukovar before the war, but after Vukovar was liberated it withdrew and they set up somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know where.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have this document before me. It's 00200457. If we can have it shown. If that is not possible, I'll continue. You say it's not possible? Very well.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's it about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You gave a more extensive statement about everything that took place in Vukovar, and I'm just going to refer to a few details. Do you remember that statement?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember where you gave the statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, this statement you would have made to the police, you say it's 20457, but we need the ERN number. The registrar needs the ERN number to be able to find this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ERN number is 0020045. The Prosecution disclosed the document to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: If I may assist. It's the 65 ter number 01328.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if you can't find it, we need not waste time on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's the document, but we don't know where you gave this statement. So the official who took the statement -- or rather the official note, compiled the Official Note, was from the police administration, the Croatian administration of Vukovar, but I don't know where the statement was made in the first place and you can't remember?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really can't remember. I don't know. If it says that I gave that statement, then I certainly did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On page 2 here, somewhere towards the middle of page 2 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have a look at page 2, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It says that in the barracks you recognised a man called Radivoje Jakovljevic nicknamed Frizider or "Fridge."

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he went from one man to the next, he would hit some of them and threatened to kill all of them?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then you say you recognised a man called Vlado Kosic who was wearing a military uniform, a JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and he used to work in the Vukovar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So he's a local, is he, over there?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I worked in the Vukovar municipality too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. I know that from the documents.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he would say, "Emil, Emil you didn't get into the right bus." And I said "Well, which is a better bus?" And he said, "It's all the same. It will be all the same."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So all these are people that you knew from before the war; right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then here you went on to explain that Colonel Mrksic was at Ovcara, but I seem to feel that you've mixed him up with another Colonel, some other Colonel, but unless you confirm that, I'm not going to pursue the point.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the name he came under. That's what was said. People said that's Colonel Mrksic. So as far as I was concerned he was Colonel Mrksic to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I see. And then you recognised another man called Bora Latinovic; right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was also wearing a military uniform, a JNA uniform; right? Or at least that's what you say here?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You say he was wearing an SMB, olive green uniform?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's the standard JNA uniform?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he boasted and said that he'd killed 50 Ustashas himself the night before?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't believe him. I don't believe that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't believe that either because the day before there weren't any of these liquidations, but you said that he boasted and bragged because he wanted to instill fear in you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't believe him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So towards the end of that page you say that on the 21st of November, in the early hours of the morning, an active JNA soldier appeared. He was a sergeant and he introduced himself as a Macedonian.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in Modateks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Modateks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I see, Modateks. So that was the following day after Ovcara, the day after you were taken to Velepromet and then transferred to Modateks?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, with him there was a young woman also wearing a JNA uniform.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you recognised her as being a local Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She is the daughter of a colleague of mine who worked together with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I see. And then you go on to say, and I'm going to quote you and that's towards the end of page 2: "I wish to stress that the sergeant was a Macedonian and that he threatened us all, and I remember this very well, when he said the following to us: You'll see what will happen when my Topola sets fire to your irises, because he allegedly has knowledge of us being the defenders of Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the truth of it. That's really what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So he introduced as -- mentioned this Topola as being one of his own?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as a subordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yesterday, you described this man Topola as being somebody who was about your height but of a little more slender build.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, but we didn't measure each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, this is why I'm asking you this, because some other witnesses when they described Topola say that this -- he was a heavily built man, 130 kilos in weight, tall and so on?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you remember him as being a man shorter than you in build?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, similar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, on 22nd of November, and that's to be found on page 3 of that statement of yours, in the early morning hours you say that an individual appeared who introduced himself as Vojvoda Vojin Misic from Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was in the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I see. And that was prior to your departure for Mitrovica; right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, before I left for Mitrovica he said -- he introduced himself and said, "I am Vojin Misic, a Serb from Negoslavci. I am going to kill you all. We're going to kill you all. We're going to throw your bodies into the Danube River, and you're going to disappear." That's what Vojin Misic said, otherwise he was a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: A JNA captain?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, anyway that's the kind of uniform he wore.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How come it says here that he was a Vojvoda?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume he said that. He probably said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He said that. Do you remember him saying that or what?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: Somebody else said that, actually, said that he was a Vojvoda, but he was one of the best dressed and most decently clad people. He had the same sort of suit that Tito wore. Now, whether this was just a show or whatever, but he was from Negoslavci, wasn't he.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's what you say?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was from Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I've never heard of him before.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had never heard of him either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I had never heard of him until I read your statement.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether he was from Negoslavci I can't say, but he introduced himself and said, "I'm Vojin Misic, a Serb from Negoslavci." That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have an unidentified statement by you here, perhaps you signed it. The ERN number is 00187079. Can you find that, please? I was disclosed that by the Prosecution, but it doesn't say when you gave that statement, to what organ, institution, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Hague OTP.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, The Hague OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They provided me with your statement. It's their duty to disclose all these documents to you.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So where's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I want to identify what statement this is and I'd like to hear from the Prosecutor what statement this is, what this is all about. What kind of statement is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: If you give me just a minute, I have to search it on the system. I will come back to this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You found the previous document. Very well. Fine. We'll deal with that while the Prosecution is dealing with the other matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So we're now going back to the Mrksic, Sljvancanin, and Radic transcripts, and we now have the page number P938, and I assume -- or, rather, 5938 and 5939. Can we see one page first and then the other? Although this doesn't seem to me to be a proper translation. The version, although I don't know English, but the version in Serbian seems somewhat different to the English. Let's have a look at 5938, first, please.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you remember where we met?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No, I don't remember having met you at all.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really? We shook hands and we talked. You were at Nikola Pekic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pekic Nikola.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Before the war?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, before the war, in the 1970s, and Nikola died quite recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't remember?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had quite a long conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What did we talk about?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, various things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I see. Various things. Well, the world is a very small place. But I hope you won't deduct that from my time, Judges. Now, have you found the page? Have you found it? Yes. It would be a good idea if the Serbian version of the transcript could be provided to the witness so Mr. Cakalic can see it. You haven't got it? Take my copy. Three lines are important on this page, and the top part I marked on the second page. And I haven't got a copy. It's not just that one copy exist, but I'll use the screen. So let's see, one page first -- or, rather, the English and the Serbian. Well, put the English version on the overhead projector so that the Judges can see for themselves first, and then put the Serbian version so that Mr. Cakalic can have a look. Let's have the English first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've seen the two pages in English. Please ask your question, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I would like to have the Serbian version put on the ELMO for Mr. Cakalic's benefit.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ha, ha.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we have the page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Take a look on that first page now. They're asking you about your testimony in -- your testimony in the Slobodan Milosevic trial, and then on page 5942, which I haven't got on my screen yet, 5942, that's the following page, towards the end of the page you see there mentioning your testimony during the Milosevic trial. Now, next page, the top of the page, please, and the man asking you the question is counsel Vasic, and he says -- yes, that's Vasic speaking. He says: "After that -- or I have to say before that on the 10th of July, 2003, you talked to members of the Ministry of the Interior, the police administration." And then you add, and these are your initials, EC, Emil Cakalic, you say: "Kastel Luksic." There's a mistake here. It's not Lukzic, it's Luksic. Then counsel says, "In Kastel, and they compiled an Official Note," and you confirm that they did and say, "Yes." Do you remember that now?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, do you remember this conversation with the Croatian police before testifying in the Milosevic trial?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were many things. There was a lot of various things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, if you don't remember, I won't insist.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What is important for me is that we have ascertained that the conversation took place. Now, I understand fully, Mr. Cakalic, that one tends to forget many things, just as I forgot ever having met you before. But I do remember every time that the police came to talk to me and when they interrogated me, and this happened very often. I remember all of that.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's why you remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. Now we're going to deal with the events in Vukovar before the war broke out, and as you have helped me out here and helped me identify and clarify the situation concerning the crime in Ovcara, I'd like to go on and say that one comes to wonder to the question of what it was that forced people who were your neighbours until all this broke out, what -- and you socialised with them and so on, what instilled this hatred in them that they appeared in Ovcara and beat the prisoners and later on some of them took part in the liquidation?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, passions were let loose.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it passions, is it ideology, what is it?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everybody views this his own particular way, but most probably it's ideology, but I would say it's passions, political passions running wild.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, is the reason -- does the reason lie in the fact that before the war, in the beginning of the conflict with the JNA, over 150 Serbs were killed on the territory of Vukovar municipality; might it be that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the first time I am hearing of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The first time. I see. Did you hear about the information centre of the Serbian Sabor or Assembly?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that there was some sort of Assembly. Whether it was the Serbian Assembly or some other, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you know that this information centre of the Serbian Assembly cooperated closely with The Hague Tribunal, with The Hague OTP?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, The Hague investigators conducted about 100 interviews and took about 100 statements from witnesses of crimes committed against the Serbs in Vukovar, and we have that on the first page of this information centre. I could provide you with the title page of this report so that the report by the information centre, Serbian information centre, can be seen. I think you were provided with this this morning, although I sent it up for translation three months ago, but may we have this report by the Serbian information centre put on the overhead projector, please. You can answer my questions in a very relaxed manner. I am not accusing you of anything. I don't have you on the list of people who committed crimes.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. You want to arrive at a truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm using documents.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'm going to help with you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. But if there is something you don't know, I won't insist.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't have a single piece of information incriminating you, so there's no reason for us to clash. You may know things, or you may not know them. On the front page you can see that this is the Serb Assembly Information Centre thereof, that they have documents testifying to the violations of human rights, ethnical cleansing, and the crimes committed by Croats against the Serbs in Croatia between 1991 and 1996. Can you see that in the heading?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have a comment if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that the Croatian people committed crimes in Vukovar or committed ill-deeds against the Serb people in Vukovar. It may well be the case, but this must have been retaliation. It was not a custom in Vukovar. We were all neighbours. We were all socialising. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, I'm not saying that the Croatian people committed crimes. The criminals are mentioned by name, Tomislav Mercep and others. It doesn't say that the people committed crimes.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, individuals and certain military forms. This is a file number 887, and title is "Crime without punishment, crimes committed by Croatian military formations against the Serb civilians in Croatia in 1992 -- 1 to 1996 and it was altered by S. Dabic and M. Lukic. On the first page of the report can you please turn to the first page. Again, this has been translated into English. The Judges must have the English translation and so do my learned friends. Your Honours, the Prosecutor has been in possession of this document for over 10 years and they have never disclosed this document to me. This is page number 1, contents, and then move on to page number 1. This is page number 1, ma'am. The OTP has never disclosed this to me according to Rule 68(i), although they are in possession of this document and I obtained this directly from the information centre of the Serbian Assembly. On page 1 paragraph 2 it says: We are from The Hague Tribunal to carry out an unbiased investigation in order to investigate the crimes committed by the Serbian people in Eastern Slavonia and Western Srem. And then there is a sentence that says in the seventh line of the second paragraph, The Hague Tribunal accepted our request and its investigation teams on four occasions between 22nd May and 2 June from 10 to 14 July, from 26 September to 1 October 1996, and from 16 to 29 January 1997, interviewed about a hundred witnesses in Vukovar. The investigation did not comprise all the crimes because there were too many crimes committed, and it was just not feasible. This file which was filed during the investigation carried out by The Hague Tribunal in Vukovar contains data and information only on the crimes about which there is enough evidence in The Hague to issue indictments against their perpetrators, members of the Croatian armed formations. Do you see that Mr. Cakalic? Do you see that sentence? What do you think about this? Do you know that this investigation did take place in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear about The Hague investigators coming to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And that they interviewed people?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, very well then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the Trial Chamber is discovering these documents with you. Apparently they had not been disclosed to the accused, which is a cause for astonishment, but on the basis of these documents, it would appear that prior to November or October 1991, in Vukovar, there were crimes committed by Croats against Serbs, and on the basis of this document there were some hundred and fifty people who fell victims. So from this document, it appears that this very Office of the Prosecutor investigated, and a witness apparently were heard. You were a resident of Vukovar. Before October and November, did you have any knowledge? Did you hear that Serbs had been victims of crimes that would have been committed by Croats, or did you never know of anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You -- I would answer as follows: The Serbs made up stories about being persecuted in order to smear the name of the Croatian people. They would flee to Vojvodina first and then to Serbia and so on and so forth. That's what they did. But the fact that Croats were killing Serbs, some were killed in duels. The person who saved me was later on killed in a duel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, these people who were killed, the list is a hundred and fifty names long. They did not kill each other in order to blame the Croats.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This was before the war, Mr. Cakalic.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This was before the war whilst different gangs under the command of Tomislav Mercep circled around Vukovar and even after he left Vukovar. I have an original Croatian document here. You have this document in a typed version because the original was not very legible. Can we have the original on the ELMO, and the Judges have a translation into English, and I'm going to be using the new typed version of this document. Mr. Cakalic, the Croatian authorities were aware of these major crimes that were committed in Vukovar, and I'm going to show you a document which is a confidential letter by Marin Vidic. Do you know him? He is a friend, I believe.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was the commissioner of the Croatian government in Vukovar. On the 18th of August, 1991 he wrote to the president of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I just want to tell you this: The Judges have not received the translation of the documents. You told us it had been translated, but we don't have the translation in front of us. So be aware that your questions cannot be enhanced by the English translation of the document. To help us -- for instance, we have a document in front of us. I can translate, and I can see that it was written on the 18th of August, 1991. Tell us who it is sent who and what was the purpose just in a nutshell so that we know what the document is about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, over three months ago I handed this over for translation to the registry, and it is not my fault if you don't have it in English. I hope that you have at least some of the things. I don't know what you have and what you don't have. And this is a letter which was the commissioner of the Croatian government for Vukovar. You know, in Vukovar there were local elections in 1990, and after the elections the president of the municipality was Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Wasn't it, Mr. Cakalic?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What is his nationality?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And how did he declare himself? He was a Yugoslav, wasn't he? Are you aware of that? Before the war he always declared himself as a Yugoslav?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? We worked together in the municipality, and I really wouldn't know. I don't know that. Maybe he declared himself as Yugoslav somewhere else, not in the workplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But it was his official position when the questionnaires had to be filled out when he had to declare his nationality, he would fill out as being Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then there was a threat that he would be arrested and he fled Vukovar sometime in July?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He went to Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then the Croatian government appointed a commissioner, Marin Vidic Bili?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Marin Vidic, on the 18th of August, wrote to the president of the republic, the prime minister of Croatia, to the minister of defence, and to the minister of the interior of Croatia, describing the political and security situation in the municipality of Vukovar. He calls this a report in Croatian. Can you see this document in front of you? I'm going to read the first part very carefully and you can follow my words. I'm going to be reading very slowly because of the interpretation. "By appointing Tomislav Mercep of the secretary of the municipal secretariat of Vukovar, the power has been usurped, and functions have been concentrated in one person, and these functions are the president of the Croatian Democratic Union, Tudjman's party, and the factical [as interpreted] command of the ZNG, the police, the civilian authorities. He is surrounded by people of dubious moral qualities, former criminals who have taken over the complete control over everything in the municipality of Vukovar and they are not shying from repressive and violent measures again the population of Vukovar. They burst into private apartments against the law. They send in to those flats by people who sought accommodation. They plunder these apartments. They seize vehicles. They bring against their will people for oppression, and they even execute people. This behaviour has created in the town of Vukovar a general psychosis of fear among both the Croatian and the Serbian population which has resulted in a mass exodus from the town, a total blockade of the work of the police, of the ZNG, the organs of the administration, and this has also created a general state of confusion. "He has brought upon himself his dismissal from the position of the secretary of the Secretariat for National Defence because it was visible that this would lead to a general catastrophe. Upon the intervention of Mr. Manolic, Tomislav Mercep has been withdrawn to Zagreb, allegedly to be the assistant minister of the interior, which has been officially published in the media." Were you able to follow my reading?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Am I reading correctly?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: "When he left Vukovar, the situation became totally confused and we have tried to dealt with the vacuum by establishing a Crisis Staff and by appointing people to important positions and by separating the authorities of the ZNG, the police, the civilian authorities, and parties. "When this started functioning, new complications arose when in incompetent people were appointed by the authorities in Zagreb; for example, the commander of the ZNG, Stjepan Radas who was dismissed, only he was a very professional and very competent person who instilled trust and who has support of the commissioner of the government of Croatia. "The Crisis Staff in Vukovar and commander of the 3rd Brigade, Mr. Vukovac; the chief of police for Slovenia, Pejic; and the coordinator for Slovenia, Baranja, Mr. Seks. Instead of him, in Arbanas was appointed and Mr. Zadro Blago, and they are people without no qualifications whatsoever, without any professional knowledge in the area. The appointment, the dismissal was carried out without any explanation at the express order of Minister Bebic. "Upon the proposal of the Crisis Staff, the acting secretary of the municipal Secretariat of Defence, the commissioner for Vukovar appointed Professor Danijel Rehak, for whom we believe that he might be able to perform this job professionally, all of a sudden received appointment on the appointment of Gazo Josip, the former Mercep's deputy. He doesn't have any professional or other qualities to perform this job. He has a high school degree, and he never served in the army. Because of this confused situation in Vukovar we are requesting your intervention, because the municipality of Vukovar is a very volatile area which threatens to be struck by an armed conflict at a larger scale and the town is almost encircled. "The appointed people are pursuing Tomislav Mercep's policies and again there is terror in town. There are armed conflicts and shooting as a manner of provocation of which may result in major consequences. The ZNG and the police and the authorities are again functioning. The former policies have created a grave psychosis of fear among the Serb and Croatian population. The complete Croatian population does not justify this sort of behaviour and they considered themselves rejected and compromised. They do not want to bear responsibility for these policies. Since we believe that we are not in a position to deal with the situation with our local forces, we are kindly asking you to send competent people urgently that would help the legal institutions of authorities and legal -- and normalise the matter. Since Mr. Bilic [as interpreted] is your personal friend, do you recognise his signature on the document?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you doubt that this is list letter?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is his letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You have heard of Mr. Tomislav Mercep, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it true that he instilled terror not only among the Serbs but also among the Croats in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the way I saw him or knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that when Tomislav Mercep left Vukovar and appointed the assistant -- assistant minister of the interior in Croatia, that he formed an armed formation that committed a mass crimes against the Serb civilians in the Pakrac valley?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that was during the war. That was during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But that was before the war. There was no war in the Western Slavonia at the time.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The war had started.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In Western Slavonia the war started some time in September 1991, or maybe even October, and this had happened before. Are you aware of this major crime against the Serb civilian?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I hear it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did the Croatian media write a lot about it? There was also a trial, and because of a procedural error the whole group was released. Do you know that he was tried for that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. I thought that he simply vanished from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Witness, this is document from the municipal authorities in Croatia at the time, so it looks like an official document, and it reports a chaotic situation, people who are incompetent, criminals. It speaks of executions. Now, this is a picture that may look like an apocalyptic picture and you were a resident and you knew everybody. What do you have to say to this, because I seem to understand that you deny all this, and here we have a very detailed document that seems to contradict what you said so far. What was the real situation prior to October 1991 in Vukovar on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The situation was critical. There were two major national groups, the Croats and the Serbs. I won't mention Ruthenians and the others, the other national minorities, ethnic minorities. If you know that this happened I believe you, but I did not know that, and I did not see that. I can only say what I saw or possibly accept someone else's ideas and thoughts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The individual who kind the document, Bilic [as interpreted], I thought you understood -- you knew him. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do. I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And he didn't tell you that as far as he was concerned it was a chaotic situation, that he had warned Zagreb of all these problems, that he wanted competent people to be appointed, that he wanted control to be taken of the situation? Did he never tell you that? Did he never tell you that people were being killed -- well, or executed, rather, if we go by the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a collaborator of Vidic. He was the president of the municipality -- not that. No, it was a different expression, a different title. But in any case, he did work for the municipality and I assisted him in that. I went to Borovo Selo and Borovo Naselje with him more than once. There were containers and rubbish bins that had been destroyed, and as a sanitary inspector I ordered that all this be dealt with quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, let's not waste any time. You told us that you worked with him, so normally you should be aware of the situation that prevailed then. This document states that people were killed, and this is the theory of Mr. Seselj, who is based on this document but also another document. And I remind you that you are under oath, and you tell us under oath that as far as you know, in Vukovar there were never crimes committed by Croats against Serbs. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see that. As I said, I did not see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That you did not see them, that's one thing, but that you may have heard about them. I'm not saying that you were on side when crimes were committed, but we want to know whether you heard of crimes, and that's quite different.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] People did speak about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're making headway. So it was spoken about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] People did speak about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you know Zdenko Novak?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was his nickname Miner?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the first time I've heard of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Stenko Novak had about a hundred kilogrammes of explosives which he used to blow up Serbian houses in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the first time I heard of this. Zdenko Novak was in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't know about his being in The Hague and I'm not interested in that. I have his name in the documents. He was a person who blew up Serbian houses. A Serb family would flee from Vukovar out of fear. He would turn up right away and blow-up their house, and this explosion would motivate other Serbs to flee as soon as they could. That was the method he used.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm surprised to hear that, because he was a very well-mannered person, a person of good character with whom I socialised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, here again we're uncovering another problem. We've heard about this -- this is the first time we're hearing about Novak. But let us imagine that a house would be blown up in Vukovar. I suppose that the residents would know that house has been blown up, and the municipality should also know about it. Did you yourself hear that Serb houses were exploded, were blown up? Prior to October 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Whenever such a thing happened, all of Vukovar knew about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were there any investigations conducted by the municipal police in Vukovar? What did the municipality do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I worked in the municipality at the time, but the municipality -- well, there was a commissioner for Vukovar municipality. His name was Marin Vidic.
