I can tell you he's a wonderful man, a very good man who wants to help everyone, and I don't believe he did anything evil, Marin Vidic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're now going to have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we're going to have a break. Mr. Seselj, you've used one hour and 10 minutes so far, so that after the break you'll have another 20 minutes to complete, to finish the cross-examination. We shall reconvene in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have resumed our hearing. Mr. Seselj, you have shown us a number of documents. I believe you are going to ask for these documents to be tendered into evidence. If we do not have the translation of these documents, we will mark these documents for identification. Let me say that a few months ago you had asked for these documents to be translated, and as things stand today you do not have the translated documents. As you have your schedule for the upcoming witnesses, perhaps -- or you do certainly know which documents you would like to show, if you send some of these documents off to be translated, you might just send them a memo and say these documents need to be translated as a priority given the witnesses who are going to come to testify. Because if you don't mention this to the translation services and if you don't prioritise your documents, well, they will continue working the way they usually do, and in that case you will not have the documents translated in a timely way. So all you need to do is tell the translation services to prioritise the translation of such and such document. So let me give you the floor back so that you can resume your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first allow me to state my position on what you have said. I don't know what the precise order of witnesses is. I don't know whether there will be any witnesses next week. I have been given some schedules by the OTP, but they never stuck to them. I don't know anything right now. When we finish with this witness, I don't know anything. I don't know whether there will be any more witnesses or not. That's uncertain. That's one point. The second point is as regards translation, you remember well that as the Pre-Trial Judge, you ordered me to find an agency on my own which is able to translate my books. I did find an agency which is reliable, which offered the lowest prices, and they were willing to do that by the end of January. The translation was not done, and you issued a new decision obliging the registry to have these two books translated by the beginning of my defence case. As of today I don't know whether there will be a defence case at all as you are kidnapping my witnesses, subpoena -- issuing subpoenas for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, to shed some light on this matter, the Trial Chamber had handed down a decision whereby you have a credit of 10.000 pages that can be sent in for translation. Unless I am mistaken, I think that was the right figure, 10.000 documents. So the Registrar must -- the registry must translate these 10.000 pages. And I stand to be corrected by my colleagues if I'm making a mistake here. We said that it was for you to tell the registrar what your priorities were. It was for you to tell them which documents should be translated first, which are a priority for you. Admittedly you did give us an estimate. We did factor all this in when we looked into the matter, and in the end we decided on the following solution: The registry will translate 10.000 pages for you overall, and then it is for you to specify which pages need to be translated first, and those will be the documents which you will want to tender into evidence. You have written some 84 books. I believe one is going to be published in the next few days, but these books are perhaps very interesting and very relevant, but it's for you to tell the registry to identify those pages which you will want to tender into evidence when the witnesses come to testify. Now, the Prosecution gave you a provisional list. Admittedly some witnesses, for whatever reason, will not be able to come to testify. Strinovic, the expert witness, for instance. But other witnesses are mentioned, and I shall not give their names because some of them are protected, are on the list. There are witness numbers. So you know who these witnesses are. And as of today already, I'm sure you know which documents you are going to be adducing through these witnesses. We also have the chart for the entire month of April. It is possible that some of the witnesses that have been scheduled are not going to come. Nonetheless, you are able to prepare this adequately. Number 34, 51, number 7, Witness 16. These are the witness numbers we have and which should enable you to prepare for them, and you can ask the translation services to have for number 34, 7, 16, and 51 to have the documents translated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I cannot prepare for all the witnesses at once. At present I don't know what witnesses are envisaged for next week or whether there will be any witnesses, nor has the Prosecutor been able to say here whether he will certainly have witnesses next week. That's one point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Seselj. Unless I'm mistaken, I believe a witness was scheduled for next week, for Thursday. I'm turning now to Mr. Mundis. There is a witness that's been planned for Thursday, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. What we're trying to do at this very moment pursuant to the oral order of the Trial Chamber yesterday is arrange for two witnesses for next week that concern Zvornik. I should have some additional information before we complete the court day today hopefully. The schedule will be circulated no later than tomorrow for next week, but we do envisage having two Zvornik witnesses for next week, assuming that we can get the authorities to act consistently with the Trial Chamber's oral order of yesterday afternoon in an expeditious manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, so as far as next week is concerned, there are two potential witnesses who are going to come and talk about Zvornik. I'm sure you have documents about Zvornik. You may have priority documents, important documents. So there are some documents you intend to tender into evidence I'm sure, because these witnesses are going to come and testify about it. I know that you are representing yourself and you're working alone. We're fully aware of that. But if you did send off some documents to the translation services that relate to Zvornik, maybe you should tell the translation services to translate one or other document, because these are extremely important documents for you, as was the document you showed us a while ago. So these documents merit to be put on a priority list. So I'll give you the floor back so that you can resume your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to use the two books to cross-examine your expert witness Ivo Tomic. I wasn't able to do that. Then I wanted to have this set of documents about Zvornik to use for the cross-examination of a great criminal that has appeared as a Prosecution witness, and I've been told that the Prosecution will have three hours for in chief and three hours for my cross-examination, whereas you changed the decision and the witness appeared under 92 ter with all -- full protective measures, completely anonymously, and I refused to cross-examine him. So that's what I needed this material for, for the cross-examination of that witness. Now I'm going to use it for the cross-examination of Mr. Cakalic who has to give the answers he can to these questions of mine; although, this was intended for quite a different witness and now Mr. Cakalic has to do this. He has not is sullied his hand in blood, Mr. Cakalic, whereas the Prosecution has put him in to this situation where I would have asked these questions of a notorious criminal, somebody that was accused of crimes against humanity and who was released from prison in an exchange with Croatian authorities. So that's the situation I have to face and I'm facing it calmly and quietly. Now, with respect to this other witness, Strinovic, I spent a lot of time preparing for him and now I see he's not coming at all, and that's a blow, and I had to check to see whether they might have sent me an expert report by him and when I went through each and every document page by page, I realised that that expert report did not exist. Perhaps this can -- these proceedings can function this way, but I don't know for how long, because my physical capabilities are limited after all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right on a number of points. This is why I asked the Prosecution last time why a witness who was on -- who was scheduled was not coming. I'm fully aware of the fact that you prepare for these witnesses. You invest a lot of time and work in this, and if you then discover that the witness is not coming, you waste a lot of time. This is why I asked the Prosecution to tell us why these changes had been made. The same applies to Mr. Strinovic who was due to come. We know now why he will not come. So I'd like you to be aware of fact that we fully understand the difficulties you come up against when it comes to preparing for these witness testimonies when they don't come. Nonetheless, the Trial Chamber has decided that the Prosecution should give us a chart which covers eight weeks, which spans a period of eight weeks, so that we get an overall understanding of which witnesses are going to come. So we want to know over a period of eight weeks which are the witnesses that are scheduled to come and testify. Mr. Mundis, can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's the first I've heard of that, Mr. President. We will certainly endeavour to do that. I'm not in a position by tomorrow to provide a schedule for the next eight weeks. Perhaps by the end of next week I would be in a position to do that. We have indicated on a few occasions in the past some of the difficulties that we've had with respect to scheduling witnesses. I'm not going to reiterate that now. I simply do want to repeat, however, that in light of the comments made by Dr. Seselj with respect to Mr. Strinovic, that was adequately addressed yesterday. We have indicated that he will not be coming in April but he will be coming at a subsequent date. I want to be absolutely clear that we have asked him to produce a new report. That report will be disclosed and not less than 30 days thereafter he will be called as a witness. So I want to be absolutely clear he is not dropped as a witness. He will be called as a witness. It's a question of him producing a revised or a better report, and then adequate time under 94 bis will be allowed before we schedule that witness I want to be absolutely clear about that. I don't believe we can take this any further at this point in time, and I would respectfully request that we move on with the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to remind you that as the Pre-Trial Judge you issued an instruction, an oral instruction, to the Prosecution to have crime base witnesses appear first and then the other witnesses and that these crime base witnesses should be grouped according to the different localities. So I assume that it would be natural that they be grouped, crime base witnesses should be grouped for Vukovar. We had a few. We'll have a few again, and then later on some more. But that's not a rational use of time and a rational presentation of evidence, let alone the problems that raises as far as I'm concerned, because I heard for the first time today that next week we're going to have crime base witnesses testifying about Zvornik, for instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Admittedly during the pre-trial stage, in order to be as rational as possible, I had indicated to Mrs. Dahl that it would be desirable for the Prosecution to call the witnesses on a municipality basis before addressing the more crucial issues, i.e., the volunteers and the individual responsibility, criminal responsibility of the accused. This seemed logical from a judicial standpoint. Mrs. Dahl heard what I said, and then I realised that she was proceeding differently. So as we have the first witnesses that are testifying, we are discussing Vukovar. Unfortunately, we shall have to move on to Zvornik, and then we shall get back to Vukovar again in a few months' time or a few weeks' time. This makes all this rather difficult to follow. I know it's difficult. I know that you have your own issues with your witnesses, but believe me, Mr. Mundis, if I were in charge of the trial and fully in charge, I would have called the Vukovar witnesses. I would then have closed the Vukovar chapter and moved on to another municipality to avoid repetitions and to avoid wasting time, to be as rational as possible. But this Tribunal operates differently. The witnesses come to discuss a municipality and then another municipality and then come back for the first municipality. I know it's a bit hotchpotch. I know that you're finding this rather difficult to call your witnesses and making sure that they can come, but if I were to prepare all this trial, I can assure you that if I had started first with the Vukovar witnesses and I wouldn't have moved on to Zvornik before I'd finished. But as the Rules of Procedure and Evidence do not entitle the Bench to control the proceedings, it is your responsibility to deal with it. And we make do with all the inconveniences here. In other words, we're going to be switching from one topic to another, and when we are concentrated on one, everybody is working in an efficient way, and in three months' time we shall get back to Vukovar again. We will have to jog our memory and so on and so forth. So that is what makes our work so difficult. But you're not responsible for this, and I am not either. This is how things work out here. Initially the people that drafted the Rules of Procedure and Evidence in 1994 should have been aware of this, but this was more than ten years ago, and it's not after ten years that you can correct all of this. So please resume, Mr. Seselj. You have 20 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, just prior to your arrival in Vukovar did anybody of the Croatian authorities, the police, or any other service talk to you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Get one thing right. I don't live in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I meant The Hague. Perhaps I made a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You live in Kastel Luksic?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did any of the Croatian authorities talk to you prior to that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody. Not with respect to your trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You didn't manage to answer one of my questions that I asked you earlier on. You said didn't know about this crime in Pakracka Poljana. Did you hear about the liquidation of more than a hundred Serbs in Gospic which was also committed by this Tomislav Mercep, the assistant minister of police of this crime? Have you heard about Gospic and the crime committed there against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The crime took place about a month before the Vukovar events.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? I had a lot of work to do at the time. I was very busy and I simply didn't have time to deal with matters like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, could Mr. Cakalic be shown page 7 of this document by the information centre of the Serbian Assembly. We have the nationality breakdown or ethnic breakdown of Vukovar because you say you know nothing specific about the crimes that took place. I'm going to try and deal with that through another witness, but as you worked in the municipality I'm sure you're well aware of things like this. So put it on the overhead projector, please, and let's have it nice and big on our screens. Have we got it now? Mr. Cakalic, this is -- well, let's see the signature and what it says under the graph. This is the national or ethnic structure of the Vukovar municipality for 1981. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And can you see that it says that in Vukovar there were 30.000-odd Croats, 25.000-odd Serbs, 18.000 people who declared themselves as Yugoslavs, and 7.800 others, Germans and various other nationalities and ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you agree that among the Yugoslavs, the largest percentage were Serbs who declared their nationality as Yugoslavs because they loved Yugoslavia? They were people from mixed marriages of course as well, but most of them were Serbs, right? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, are you aware that at the first multi-party elections in 1990, the Croatian Democratic Union; that is to say, Tudjman's party in Vukovar was completely defeated?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you provide this document to Mr. Cakalic, and then we can look at the text, the excerpts I underlined.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the graph first, and what it says underneath, the caption underneath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Seselj. I see that when you put the question on the elections in 1990, where you say that Tudjman's party was defeated, he didn't answer. There was no answer on the part of the witness. So could you ask your question again if you feel that this is an important question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness nodded in the affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I asked you whether you remember that the Croatian Democratic Union was defeated in Vukovar in 1990.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that it was such a resounding defeat. The Croatian Democratic Union lasted for as long as Professor Tudjman was alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: While Senada is continuing the work. It's still alive today, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but we're talking about individuals of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Look at this graph. These are the results of the elections in Vukovar municipality in 1990 according to the number of seats won in the Municipal Assembly. Can you see that? Can you see these figures? The League of Communists of Croatia had 64.55 per cent; right? The HDZ, which is Franjo Tudjman's party, had secured 26.22 per cent of the seats in the municipality; and the other parties and independent candidates scored 27.23 per cent.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that correct? Do you doubt this? Is that the true?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say that it isn't, that it isn't right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What are your figures then?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the HDZ was the strongest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And how many deputies did it have in the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh I really can't say I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you think they were the strongest you say?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were the strongest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why did they elect Slavko Dokmanovic as president of the Municipal Assembly if the HDZ was the strongest?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the area of Vukovar has a mixed population. You are very much aware of that yourself. There are Croats and Serbs and national minorities, Ruthenians and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. We saw that on the last graph. But why would the HDZ, if it were indeed the strongest, elect a Serb who belongs to the League of Communists, the party for Democratic Change?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes he was an SDP candidate?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was indeed an SDP candidate and was the president of the municipality who didn't go home. He went across the Danube to Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We're not talking about him now. But your thesis, that the HDZ had the majority, whereas from this graph we see that it did not, that it was in the minority in the Municipal Assembly. Now look at what it says, what the text says, the Information Centre of the Serbian Assembly and the document that the OTP of The Hague has in its position -- possession. I'm going to read the text slowly and you can give me your comments: "The Croatian Democratic Union has suffered a complete defeat at the multi-party elections in Vukovar in 1990, principally because the Serbs and the so-called Yugoslavs who together made up an absolute majority of the population in this town and its surrounding parts, voted for the League of Communists of Croatia party for Democratic Change candidate. "In the Vukovar municipality, five deputies for the Sabor Assembly of the Republic of Croatia were elected, four deputy seats were taken by the Party of Democratic Change and one place by the so-called independent candidate. In the Assembly of the Vukovar municipality, which had 117 deputy seats, the Croatian Democratic Union won just 26 mandates. It only won in settlements where the -- there was an absolute Croatian majority population." Is that correct, Mr. Cakalic?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a relative question, but if this was recognised by somebody from Croatia, then I do believe that that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: These are official data of the Croatian authorities after the elections?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the figures for 1990. There are three main groups, the SDP, the HDZ, and the independent parties, and there are election results which nobody can challenge. This is not a relative matter. Out of the 117 elected MPs, the HDZ has 26, which from a mathematical standpoint tends to indicate that the SDP is in the majority. League of Communists. So you seem to be challenging this. This is -- these are the results of the elections.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As to the results, I accept them. However, it was a little strange to me -- well, I didn't delve in politics at all as you well know, I dealt with my profession, so I assume that what it says here is correct. I do believe it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You worked in the municipality did you not? You were in the municipality administration?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the sanitary inspector for the municipality of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you were a municipality official?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it true and correct, Mr. Cakalic, that in the Vukovar municipality five deputies were elected to go to the Croatian Sabor Assembly?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It says here that five deputies for the Sabor, the parliament, were elected, and not a single one of them was from the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union. Four were from the SDP, the Party of Democratic Changes, and one seat was taken by an independent candidate?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know of an HDZ deputy from Vukovar? This wasn't a single one.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was -- oh, help me. What was his name. He came from Lovas, Marin Vidic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What party did Marin Vidic belong to?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he belonged to the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was he a deputy in the Croatian parliament?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No. He was a municipal official because the offices in the municipality were divided proportionally according to ethnic affiliation?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But he was not a deputy in the parliament?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He became the commission of the Croatian government for Vukovar when Slavko Dokmanovic fled Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to look at the following text?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could there be a pause between question and answer please, the interpreters kindly request.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Look what it says here: A defeat in the elections in Vukovar municipality prompted the leadership of the Croatian Democratic Union --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please slow down. The interpreters find it difficult to follow you at this speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Prompted the leadership of the Croatian Democratic Union to attempt to render null and void the results of the elections in this municipality by suspending the legally elected organs of the local authorities and transferring their powers on to a so called commissioner of the Croatian Government. How was it possible to achieve this? Only under irregular conditions. The government authorities of the Republic of Croatia were intentionally provoking Serb-Croatian confrontations. Well, let me just mention one thing. In the footnote here it says, "Report on the results of the elections in Vukovar municipality," and this was published in the Vukovar newspaper of the 12th of May. Can you see this footnote? Could you please turn the next page please. Is this the next page? I have the next page. I have the next page. You were showing the previous page now. There was another important reason which prompted the Croatian authorities to work on a speedy, even a forcible takeover of power in Vukovar municipality because most of the population of Vukovar was composed of Serbs and declared Yugoslavs, Vukovar could become a serious flashpoint and a serious centre of resistance to the Republic of Croatia. Seen from the standpoint of the Croatian government, this danger was even greater because of the geographical position of the Vukovar municipality which bordered on the territory of the Republic of Serbia which at that time opposed the break-up of Yugoslavia. Do you agree with this assessment of the situation? Could you please give me this document back, because now I miss it and there's something important on it.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were very many people who were Serbs but were not Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They declared themselves as Yugoslavs?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there were also Croats to declared themselves as Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There were such Croats as well, especially from mixed marriages?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But they were all in favour of the survival of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who was in favour of what.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There was some Croats who fled Vukovar because of Tomislav Mercep and his gangs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you don't even know about the Serbs. What can we do? I can't force you to know --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I'm telling you what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear of some powerful and wealthy Mafia bosses who moved to Vukovar in 1989? This was the Alco Mafia. They produced alcohol from cereals and traded it in illegally.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it rings a bell but I couldn't swear to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard of Marin Pliso?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Vinko Zanic?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Josip Dufek?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were they the wealthiest and most powerful bosses of the Alcohol Mafia?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it was the Alco Mafia, I don't know. But even today they trade in wine and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did they begin to gather around themselves workers who were out after job and criminals, and did they start creating their own armed groups the members of which obeyed them without question in order to secure their livelihoods? It says that these groups became the mainstay for the Croatian Democratic Union, a branch of which was set up in Vukovar in March 1990. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know when a poor person gets a job he has to work, and he has to do whatever his boss tells him to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember those first armed formations of the HDZ in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember when people began procuring weapons in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was it as early as 1990?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I couldn't tell you the year, but people started obtaining weapons. Why? Well, because the army was there in Vukovar and people had to keep themselves safe. Everyone who to protect himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was the army threatening anyone in Vukovar in 1990?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was the army threatening anyone?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why then would people have to obtain weapons?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who, the army?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No, the civilians, the Alco Mafia, the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that the HDZ procured weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, who procured weapons?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Mafia. You yourself said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But we can see from this document that this Mafia was the mainstay of the HDZ in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you believe what this document says?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Relatively.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I believe you have two or three minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Cakalic, who the first victim was on the territory of Vukovar municipality, the first person who was killed? Let me remind you.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the 1st of May, 1991, in the village of Brsadin not far from Vukovar, that's Vukovar municipality, a Serb, Stevan Inic, was killed. He was born in 1928 and he was killed by a pistol shot to his head. He was killed by Croat Djuro Gelencir, a member of the party militia of the Croatian Democratic Union. Have you heard of this murder?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear there was a murder, but I don't know who committed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In Brsadin?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Brsadin. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And in this document it says that with his murder, which resounded among the Serbs, the first step was taken into the hell of inter-ethnic war.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that prominent Serbian politicians at the time were Goran Hadzic and Borivoje Savic who came from that area?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were from Borovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's also Vukovar municipality isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And they were members of the SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But they belonged to the moderate wing of the SDS as it was called?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know then why they fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you know what happened to them on 31st of March 1991 in Plitvice on the road to Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There they were arrested by the Croatian police who beat them up on the spot, who beat them up very badly, and then they transformed a peacemaker into an extremist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, do you want us to have the transcript of your cross-examination or is it something we don't actually need?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because you're speaking extremely fast, and at page 65, line 5, you can see that on your screen, part of the question has not been recorded. I don't know. Afterwards the court reporters may be able to complete the transcript, but for the time being we have no idea about the exact substance of your question. The witness answered, "Yes I do," but we don't actually know what your question was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President and Ms. Lattanzi, there's a specific problem here. I know that very often I speak too fast. I cannot think about the interpreters and the transcript at every point. It's impossible. I'm doing my best, and I will continue to do my best. But independently of this, there are enormous problems in interpretation which I have pointed out more than once. I think the best thing to do would be for you, as the Trial Chamber, to hand down an order after every session to compare every transcript with the videotape and to have corrections entered on this basis. I do not receive the transcript. I have nothing to do with the transcript. All I get is the video, and in my view what I have is what is on the video. Then my service takes this down on paper and I use it as my own transcript. But I think that there should be a check of the transcript after each session. I'm not sure this is done. But I will slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You know that Croatian television intentionally filmed their arrest and beating?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Of Goran Hadzic and Savic on the 31st of March near Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They hadn't fled yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No, no, that's the 31st of March 1991. They were moving around Croatia freely?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They were arrested and their arrest and the brutal conduct of the Croatian police towards them, as it says on page 13 of this document, was intentionally filmed with a TV camera and shown that same evening on Croatian state television, which was under the complete control of Tudjman's party, and this caused enormous fear in all the Serbian villages. They saw them brutally mistreating a couple of moderate Serbs. What then would they do with the nationalists?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Sremska Mitrovica, and you know who beat me up? Goran Hadzic and Boro Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's possible this happened.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's quite possible, Mr. Cakalic, but this simply proves my point. Some of those who beat you up in Sremska Mitrovica, of course there are psychopaths on every side always who beat people up for no reason, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But there are people who have been harassed, mistreated, or who had a close relative or family member killed, and they are blinded by an irrational desire for revenge. Maybe the two of them were like that in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were a few like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, my point is that when someone is powerful and strong like Aleksandar Vasiljevic, and he orders 200 Croatian prisoners to be shot, it wasn't hard to find perpetrators among the local Serbs, people who were willing to do this because their house had been blown up, a family member had been killed, they had been mistreated and they longed for revenge. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Cakalic. I'm very pleased with your testimony. You have acquitted yourself honourably as a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we move on to redirect, I for one have two very short questions to put to you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've just realised that Mr. Goran Hadzic and Boro Savic were arrested by the Croats and mistreated. A crew of the Croatian television filmed the scene, and it is my understanding that Goran Hadzic and the other one, these two individuals who were arrested, it is my understanding that they mistreated you whilst you were being detained in Mitrovica. Can you confirm that for us?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when they mistreated you, were they avenging themselves after what had been done to them, or it was for an entirely different reason?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me move on to my second question, which is more important than the first one. Following the questions that were put to you, we find that the Vukovar municipality had a commissioner from the government who was in charge of managing the municipality after the departure of Slavko Dokmanovic. Mr. Dokmanovic left for Vojvodina. You told that yourself. And as a result, Mr. Dokmanovic was no longer the president of the municipality. You also said in answer to questions put to you by the Prosecutor, you said that in Ovcara Mr. Dokmanovic was there. He was on the scene. You even said that he talked to you.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If what you say is true, I would like to know the following: In what capacity was Mr. Dokmanovic on the scene, because he was not the president of the municipality. Apparently he was not a JNA officer either. He had left Vukovar. Therefore, he apparently was not playing any part in the Territorial Defence unless he had been a Chetnik or a volunteer. Can you tell us from your point of view what it's all about, because you said Dokmanovic was there. In what capacity was Dokmanovic there?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened at Ovcara when the Croats were captured and deported to the hangar, the hangars where they sent us and where they mistreated us. This Dokmanovic was at the door leading into the hangar, and every prisoner who entered through that door, not each and every one, but many of them were beaten up by Slavko Dokmanovic, the president of Vukovar municipality. This is a disgrace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I understand what happened. You told us about it. Mr. Seselj is not challenging it. But the Judges have a question in their mind. At least I have a question. What was Mr. Dokmanovic doing there? Because we know you told us that he had left his position in the municipality, had been replaced. How come he came back? Do you have an explanation for this, or maybe not?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was desire on his part to beat up as many Croats as possible. He kicked them and he had shoes on. He kicked me too. And many of our lads were beaten up by Dokmanovic for as long as Dokmanovic had any strength left. Then he left. But whether he was in Vojvodina -- well, he did come there when we were taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, you cannot tell me whether he was a member of the JNA, the TO, whether he was a Chetnik. The only thing you can tell me is that he was there, but you do not know why he was there and in what capacity.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he was a Chetnik. I'm sure that he was a Chetnik. If he had not been a Chetnik he would not have done the things that he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if he was really a Chetnik, was he wearing a special kind of hat? Were there any distinguishing features about him or -- and this is my final question: Or according to you is it so that everyone who is not a Croat is a Chetnik?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I deny that. But Slavko Dokmanovic came to Ovcara as a Serb, as a former president of the municipality of Vukovar, and there was no dignity in that, in him coming to Ovcara as the former president of Vukovar and beat his own fellow citizens. He lost all credibility with me, and I never bothered to say hello to him after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Unfortunately we won't be able to put questions to him because he died. I believe that he hanged himself in his cell, unless I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In The Hague, yes, he hanged himself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you raised this question beyond the scope of the examination-in-chief and the cross. He was mentioned, but neither the Prosecutor nor I insisted too much on Dokmanovic's case, but you have to bear in mind that in one of the courtrooms a video footage was shown which showed that at the relevant time Dokmanovic was at a different place, that he gave a statement to a TV station, and you could see that the time and the date of that statement were depicted and he was in civilian clothes. So in my view it was not very important for me to question this witness with this regard, because Slavko Dokmanovic is no longer with us. But you have to bear that in mind, and the Prosecutor's office are aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. This has been recorded in the transcript. Before I give the floor to the Prosecution for redirect, Mr. Seselj, are you requesting MFI numbers for the two documents you produced?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like all the documents to be identified, and it is up to you. And I'm very disappointed with your decision that the 180 documents that refer to the Sarajevo theatre of war should not be admitted. So I'm really resigned. I'm not asking for anything. You do whatever. It is up to me to offer documents, to show them, and it is up to you to either adopt them or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Registrar, give us some MFI numbers for the documents shown by Mr. Seselj to the witness. I'm talking about MFI numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The first document was the Vukovar municipality document dated the 18th of August, 1991. That will be MFI D17. And the second document is the Serbian Council Information Centre document which will be MFI D18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Seselj, to conclude, you told us that you were extremely disappointed because the Trial Chamber decided not to admit the 180 documents you submitted with respect to Sarajevo and the Sarajevo theatre of war. You will be in a position to put these documents to other witnesses. They're not lost. But please produce them at the right time. That's all I had to say about this. These documents will come back inevitably. I'm turning now to the Prosecutor. Do you have any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I have a very short redirect, but I have three topics where I want to make some annotations. I think it's not the first time that we got to the documents from the Accused in the morning or at the moment when cross-examination starts, and I think this is unfair to the Prosecution and also to you Judges. It should have been given to us well in advance that we have at least have an opportunity to see what these documents are about. I don't care if they are not in English. I have the possibility to go through them with a language assistant to at least know what they are about. This is my observation to this point. I have a second observation. Mr. Seselj mentioned this video about Dokmanovic. It's true. I have this -- I remember this video. We have it in our possession and we will play this in due time. As far as I remember, Mr. Dokmanovic is seen there in civilian clothes, but this is in the afternoon and not at the evening. We will see this when it's opportune to look at them. Another point I want to make, Mr. Seselj, when he started cross-examining Mr. Cakalic, he said at the beginning, it's at page 2, lines 12 to 15, and I read from the transcript: "Your Honours, I think this is an important issue, and it's not the first time that the Prosecution asks for protective measures without the witness having requested." I want to make clear that we never asked for protective measures for Mr. Cakalic. He has always been under his name. It's true that he has a pseudonym. This was more or less for technical reasons, but we did not use it, and we never asked for protective measures for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When Mr. Seselj said that, it caught my attention, as you can imagine. When you prepare your 65 ter lists with all the witnesses, why are all these lists always confidential, whereas some witnesses never ask for any protective measures and whereas some of these witnesses have already testified in open session in other trials? So why do you file these lists confidentially, and why are there pseudonyms sometimes on these lists? There was nothing preventing you from stating right from the beginning that Cakalic was going to testify without any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: This was the decision of the former senior trial attorney in this trial -- in this procedure. She decided to have all the witnesses on the 65 ter list with pseudonyms. This is all I can tell you about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Please put your questions. Oh, no. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the first statement that was provided to me that was signed by Mr. Cakalic was under a pseudonym. The first statement. That was submitted to me by the Prosecutor's office. That was signed by Mr. Cakalic. It was under a pseudonym, and I could not see his signature. It was only subsequently that they published his name. They are the ones who give pseudonyms only to protected witnesses. I have a list of witnesses who are not protected and who do not have any pseudonyms, and you can see that from the last list that was submitted to us by the Prosecutor's office on the -- of the trial, which means that for a long time Mr. Cakalic was a protected witness of the OTP under seal, and I could not disclose his name in public up to the moment when Mr. Cakalic appeared in the courtroom and when it became apparent that he wanted to be a public statement. And this is not the first time that this has happened. We had other witnesses who said that they didn't -- didn't ask for any protective measures, and it was only in the courtroom that they appeared in public. And this is all on purpose to thwart the preparation of my defence, because from the statement given by Mr. Cakalic, I didn't know who the person was. I was only aware of the event and the description but I did not know that it was Mr. Cakalic, so I couldn't investigate who he is, what he did during the war, whether I can put his credibility in question. Mr. Cakalic, we do that in order to test the credibility of a witness. And this was something that I was prevented from doing for years, and now on the eve of the trial I had a lot of disclosed names and then I got lost trying to find information about each and every one of these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I could agree with you in part regarding what you've just said, but I totally disagree as to the fact that you could not know that this witness was going to be Mr. Cakalic. Indeed, you received the transcripts of his testimony in the Milosevic case, in the Dokmanovic case, as well, in the Martic [as interpreted] case. Therefore, by comparing you could imagine that the witness being given a pseudonym was in fact Mr. Cakalic, because if he in the Milosevic case said that he was in the Ovcara farm where he was beaten up, and if he said that Mr. Dokmanovic was present there, if that is repeated in the Dokmanovic case transcript, and if you discover that there is a witness with a pseudonym who says that he was beaten up in the presence of Dokmanovic, I mean, you don't need to have invented the wheel to conclude that this was Mr. Cakalic. So I may agree with you in part. However, as to your conclusion, I do not quite agree with you. I mean, you are very knowledgeable about this case, and it would have been easy for you to guess that this was Mr. Cakalic. Yes, please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it was only recently that I received transcripts of Mr. Cakalic's testimony in other trials, and this was definitely after the beginning of my trial. I can't tell you exactly when but the OTP will have those dates. But it was recently. Everything from November on is actually recently. But during the five years while I was preparing for my defence, I was not in a position to prepare properly because they denied me the names of almost all witnesses. All of their statements were under pseudonym. And I claim that this was done on purpose. I fully believe that this was done on purpose. They even wanted to have this witness as a 92 ter. They did not want to -- to have him say anything. When they have a 92 ter, they just show him photographs, ask him whether they saw this or that, as if somebody denied that Ovcara was where it is or Velepromet or barracks or the hospital in Vukovar. This is just nonsense, nothing else. There are other things which are more important than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, Mr. Seselj, the Trial Chamber has heard your objections regarding the 92 ter procedure. You know that we have 92 ter witnesses that were scheduled as such, and we have decided to hear them in court maybe in the future. I know that you'll react to that negatively, but unfortunately there's no other way around. There may be other 92 ter witnesses. And once again I'm pointing it out to you. Even though there may be some drawbacks to the 92 ter proceedings, it is of a great advantage to the accused in that he is entitled to cross-examine and to submit documents to the witness. That's the general regime, the general economy as it were of this 92 ter proceeding. Do you have any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I have one, but allow me to make one remark. I'm -- Mr. Seselj said that he was not able to publish the name and maybe also the statement of the witness. I have serious concerns about this publishing of names of witnesses and their statements before they come into the courtroom and testify here in the courtroom. If it is done after, then it's okay. In my system where I am from, and I'm sure that it's also in the other civil law systems, this would be a crime; publishing the name and the statement of a witness who didn't testify in open session. This is my remark to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj. What did you mean by that when you said publish the names? Maybe there was a problem around the translation, but what did you mean exactly, because the Prosecutor is somewhat concerned. The fact that you know that a witness is about to testify in open session, if that is published, do you intend before that witness appears to say to the press, "Mr. XYZ is going to come and speak about this"? That's the concern expressed by the Prosecutor. What do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the first time I saw Mr. Mussemeyer in one of the courtrooms he looked worried to me. He's always worried. Every document that I receive either from the Prosecutor's office, from the Trial Chamber or the registry that doesn't bear the confidentiality seal is a public document. I have the right to publish it on my internet site. I have the right to show it to the public just like the Prosecutor's office does. For example, if the first statement provided by Mr. Cakalic had been given to me in the Serbian under his name, it is my right to give this to my team of investigators to go to the field and to inquire among the people who Mr. Cakalic is. If I only have a pseudonym, I can't send my investigators to the field with that pseudonym. I have obtained a lot of statements here owing to the TV broadcast of the trial and people contacted my investigators and told them this witness is lying. And what about this confidentiality? If it is not a shame to testify, but when they provide a false testimony which is a common practice because it is the Prosecutor's office that provides them with false statements that they repeat, then I have to intervene. My only defence is the defence of the general public. I don't have any other defence before this Trial Chamber, and the only thing that I rely on is the judgement of the general public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In making this observation you raise a problem for which I or the Chamber has no solution. Mr. Seselj has a web site on which he displays information regarding his trial, publically so. So the issue appears to be as follows: What would happen were Mr. Seselj to publish in his web site things about a hearing or evidence before a witness comes to testify? I have no answer to that. I know that in civil law countries such as mine before a witness appears Defence can say -- can say that such-and-such a person is about to appear and we plan to ask such-and-such questions about him or her and this is being done publicly. So you express a concern which I personally cannot meet. Neither can the Trial Chamber probably. So there it is. I mean, we are in a world of communication. You know that the trial proceedings are broadcast with a time lag of 30 minutes. It is broadcast on the internet. Everybody knows what is happening. I believe that Channel 2 as of 10.00 p.m. in Belgrade broadcast part of the hearing. This is it. This is the world of speed, of information, of media, and this of course may go against the very principle of judicial proceedings, but I have no solution to that. You can always file a motion before the Trial Chamber, and the Trial Chamber will hand down a decision. But let's move to the heart of the matter. That was your redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Exactly, but a short answer. For the witnesses who are expected to come here to testify, to read already in the books their whole statement and to have comments on them which are not very positive is for me a kind of harassment. This is my personal opinion. I don't want to continue on this but just for you to know. I can put a question. I have only one question to Mr. Cakalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, does the name Colonel Mrkusic say something to you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was also in the Hague, Mrkusic, Sljvancanin, and Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Is it possible that they --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Is it possible that you were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, are we talking about Mrkic, Mrkusic? It's not very clear. We have various spellings to that name in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I referred to the person, to the Colonel who was in the hangar blowing the whistle every time when there was a change of the beating persons. The witness said this was captain Mrksic, which is not correct. He may have mixed it up. I asked him if he knows Colonel Mrkusic, and according to my information this colonel in the hangar who was blowing the whistle was not Colonel Mrksic but his name was Colonel Mrkusic, and the witness said this in his statement of 1995 on page 7. This is all I want to let you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cakalic, I want to thank you on behalf of my colleagues. Thank you for coming to testify as a Prosecution witness. You've come here several times. I hope this was the last time. Madam usher is going to help you get out of the room, the courtroom. We'll have the 20-minute break now. And we're going to have video clips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing's resumed. Today's and tomorrow's hearing are going -- hearings are going to be devoted to video viewing, and we're going to do it as follows: Before a video clip is shown, the Prosecutor will give us the date it was done, the origin of it, and the subject of the video and possibly the length of it. Everybody's going to view the footage. Thereafter, I shall give the floor to Mr. Seselj, who may make some observations, telling us why he opposes the video clip. Failing any opposition, the Trial Chamber will give a final number. Should be there a challenge, there will be an MFI number given to the footage. As a result, the Prosecution will have to submit the footage again at a later time through another witness. Just to meet a criticism that may be raised, namely that a video clip may give a snapshot taken out of the whole context of the video as such and that therefore that may be given a different interpretation, of course this observation is taken on board by all the Judges, but if such cases were to arise, the Prosecution will always have the opportunity to show us the entire video footage when a witness comes to testify and the accused will also be given an opportunity to show the entire video to support his case or in cross-examination of another witness. I remind you that the fact that a document is admitted does not mean that we thereby give a great probative value to the document. You must make a distinction between the admission and the probative value of a document because the probative value is assessed only at the end of the trial. Therefore, any discussion on a given document may waste time, because the probative value of a document is only assessed at the end of the trial proceedings once the Defence has made its case as well through its own documents, so that a document that may be initially of great relevance may turn out at the it end to be without any relevance. The other way around as well. A document that may have not initially any relevance may turn out to be extremely relevant as time goes by, but we only know this at the end of the process. I say and say it again: If you start firing to try and destroy a document, there's no point to it, because this sort of barrage fire is only useful when a document is challenged as to its authenticity. If you claim that it's been manipulated, that it is a fake document, if you challenge the authenticity then it's okay. But apart from such cases, I fail to see why a document could or should be challenged. Yes, Mr. Seselj, you wanted to intervene before we see the clips?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, the Prosecutor prior to the break made a potentially very important statement, and I think he would be duty-bound to state his views on that -- on the matter before you. We saw that this witness whose testimony has just been completed spoke about Colonel Mrksic as a man who was present at Ovcara. He called him Mrkusic, Mrkusic, and it's a notorious fact established in other trials that Colonel Mrksic wasn't in Ovcara at all and that's something that the Prosecution knows full well. And then the Prosecutor said that the witness isn't in fact say Mrksic but Mrkusic. We know that the witness said Mrkusic thinking of Mrksic, but I demand that the Prosecutor state his position straight away and tell you whether he has certain knowledge that a Colonel Mrkusic exists at all who could have been at Ovcara at the relevant time. Has the Prosecutor established that Colonel Mrkusic actually does exist? I think this is an extremely important point, so that we know that the Prosecutor isn't perhaps speaking off the top of his head. So please would you ensure we hear the Prosecutor on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question put to the witness, and the witness answered it, was whether there was a Colonel Mrkusic who was present, if I understood properly. He was the one who was blowing the whistle. Is that right? That's what I understood. What is it, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I am not aware if a Colonel Mrkusic really exists. I only can judge from the statements I am aware of, and I realised while reading through the statements of Ovcara that there was very often a mix between Mrksic and Mrkusic, and I tried to find this out, and I found out from the statement of the witness Cakalic that he in his statement from 1995, on page 7, used the name Mrkusic. If a colonel like this really exists, I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, here you have proof of a fantastic manipulation. It is quite obvious that this witness is confusing the name of Mrkusic and Mrksic, and that is understandable for a witness of this age and physical and mental condition that he's in. And I'm sure that the witness is not doing this through any ill-intent. The Prosecution knows full well that his colleagues provided this witness a number of photographs, a large number of photographs, to point out Colonel Mrksic, and the witness was not able to do that, and it was stated in the Milosevic trial by the Prosecutor. The witness was not able to identify Mrksic. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (redacted) don't know whether Colonel Mrkusic exists. You know why they don't know? Because this person does not exist as having been at Ovcara. There was a colonel and we are going to establish in due course who that colonel was and check out why the Prosecution is protecting that colonel, but there's no doubt about the fact that Mrksic was not there. That's been established quite definitely. There was a colonel and now we'll go and investigate and see which colonel. And I have another comment and observation to make, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. While you were speaking, I was having a look at the written statement by Mr. Cakalic. It was given on the 18th of June, 1995. And the investigator is Vladimir Dzuro. Apparently the interview took place in a hotel. And on all pages we see mention -- mention of Colonel Mrksic. The first mention is on page 6. It is then repeated on several occasions. On page 7, as you said, Mr. Prosecutor. So Colonel Mrkusic is mentioned on several occasions. Well, the witness was not able to answer those questions, but did he think of Colonel Mrksic, or did he have another colonel in mind? We don't know that at all, only this: The only one who might have shed some light was the investigator interviewing him, Mr. Vladimir Dzuro. I guess that he -- he knew the players, as it were, in Vukovar. And if the witness said Colonel Mrkic or Colonel Mrkusic, the investigator must have checked that, must have checked the accuracy of the name. I don't know that investigator. I guess that he was a professional investigator who had a basic knowledge of the facts. So when that name was mentioned by the witness, he must have checked at least. So that's it. At this stage, we have no knowledge. Was the witness confused or not? I don't know. No conclusion can be drawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: To avoid further confusion, I would like to ask the Prosecution if it is the Prosecution's position that Colonel Mrksic was present in Ovcara at the relevant time, because if that is not the case, then there's no reason to venture much further into this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I personally have no information if he was there. I believe he wasn't there. This is what I infer also from the lecture of the judgement in the Vukovar -- in the so-called Vukovar three case. But as I already said, I realise that there was a confusion with names, and I saw that in the statement of Mr. Cakalic it was mentioned a Colonel Mrkusic who was blowing the whistle, and this is all the information I have about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand, but if the Prosecution and the Defence are in agreement that Colonel Mrksic was not present in Ovcara it at that relevant time, then I think that solves one difficulty in this proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you look at page 6 of this interview that gave rise to the written statement by this witness, normally speaking we should be able to find a solution, because towards the middle he said this: "At that juncture a colonel whose name I didn't know, but I learned it later, I learned his name in the case of Mitrovica," and he then gives the name of Mrkusic. So at first the witness said that he didn't know the colonel's name, and then he said that he learned it was Colonel Mrkusic, which he connected to Mitrovica. And then the witness added: "I saw a picture of the colonel. I recognised the man as being the colonel in Ovcara. And underneath the picture there was a name, the name of Colonel Mrksic." So he said that he saw a picture with Colonel Mrksic. That's it. So upon reading this I have the impression that he was speaking about this colonel, because allegedly this colonel was also in Mitrovica. The Prosecutor is telling us that he can't say whether this was Colonel Mrksic. I guess that the Vukovar Trial Chamber looked into this matter and tried to ascertain whether Colonel Mrksic was present or not. So we just have to look at the Vukovar judgement. Let's move on to something else. What else did you want to say, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, just one sentence with respect to what we were saying. I think that the Prosecutor is duty-bound to inform the Trial Chamber, me as the accused, which colonel it is or higher officer, perhaps he was a lieutenant colonel, but anyway which one was in Ovcara at the relevant time. I think the investigators of the OTP should know that. That's the least they should know. Now, with respect to the videotapes to be shown today, pursuant to your instructions the Prosecutor on the 18th of March disclosed to me a review of these videotapes in Serbian. Just before I entered court today, or just now after this break, after our break, I received a new breakdown of the videotapes in English where the order has been changed, the order in which the videos will be shown, and I don't know whether some new videotape has been introduced or not. Since this is in English, I demand that you issue instructions to the Prosecutor now that the order has been changed, I managed to establish that, that this be translated into Serbian this afternoon. It's not a big job. And then we can start showing the tapes tomorrow morning, because I can't follow on the basis of what I've been given. I'll lose more time trying to find where the videotape is than the videotape itself. If we're seeing 30 seconds, a minute, a minute and a half of tape, I don't have enough time to do anything. So may I be provided with this same document in the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm turning to the Prosecution team. I now discover what Mr. Seselj has just mentioned. We had a first document, a list of video clips. The first video had a 65 ter number, 1836, and then there was 6063. Now we have a new document with a different order. Look at the first video clip. It would be now 65 ter number 6063. That was number 2 in the previous list, and now we have 6005 as number 2 in this list, and that was on page 2 in the first place. Why, Mr. Mundis, did you change the whole lot?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In fact, we -- what we have done is not -- certainly not added any tapes or added any material. What we have done was to slightly reorganise it in terms of themes, if you will, that would make it a little bit easier to follow in terms of evolving themes contained in the videotapes. So what they have simply -- what we've simply done is put them into a slightly different order than they were before, and that's what this table reflects. Nothing has been added. There are no new tapes on this list compared with the list that was circulated yesterday. They're simply -- they've simply been put into a different order based on themes which are visible in bold at the top of the description -- of the subcategories of the descriptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. In this new list in English we also have some Serb parts, some parts in Serbian. The first theme is that of the volunteers in Vukovar and cooperation with JNA TO. That's the first thing. And under this topic we have several video clips. The second theme, on page 5, is that of Mr. Seselj and his Vojvodas. Under this heading we have several clips as well. Third topic, Mr. Seselj and the Muslims. Fourth topic, the JCE and the way -- and organisation of volunteers. The last topic being Mr. Seselj and his defence at the ICTY. Are these the topics you identified?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is precisely what I identified in terms of re-organising them under themes. Those are precisely the subtopics or themes, if you will, of videotapes on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, with regard -- compared to the first list -- there are two changes. First, you have put together videos by themes, and you reshuffled the order in the videos. These are the only two changes. Now, Mr. Seselj, you're not going to now to claim that these changes will make it impossible for you to prepare for the viewing. I would find it hard to believe.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, Judge, sir, regardless of the fact that you can't -- you find it hard to believe, I cannot follow those videotapes because I have not received the list in the order in which they're going to be shown. You have the privilege of receiving it all in English. I have not received a document in the proper way, so may I have this provided in Serbian. There's not a single word here in Serbian here except the title -- or, rather, the names. And then the tapes can be shown tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, by this afternoon, I know you have of an assistant who speaks Serbian, could you send this list in Serbian to Mr. Seselj? He would have the whole afternoon to view the video clips he has already. We have time tomorrow. As I told you, we've got basically one hour of viewing. There will be comments and observations. It will take more time, but in theory, we should be able to finish it all tomorrow. And we had basically another 45 minutes, so it wouldn't be much of a problem to stop now. What do you think, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, that that will in fact be done, and I would expect it would take us no significant period of time in order to simply cut and paste from the prior list and put them in the right order. Let me -- let me just add one other factor, because that might cause the list or could cause the list to be reduced in terms of the number of videos. As Your Honours will note, there are a few of these video tapes that appear on this list which have already been admitted into evidence, and I believe these were the videotapes that were shown during Dr. Seselj's testimony in the Milosevic case. The first three, in effect, if you will, on the first page, have already been admitted into evidence. With respect to the videos --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm -- I thought of it overnight. You know, like all of you, I work during the night as well, and I wondered. I said, what does that mean, "have been admitted into evidence in the Milosevic case"? Did you file a written motion for the videos to be admitted, to be admitted by our Chamber? Is that the way I should understand things?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It's my understanding, Mr. President, that when the transcripts of Mr. Seselj's testimony in the Milosevic case were admitted that these videos came along with that. The exhibits and materials that came along with that. In effect, it was an entire package so that the prior testimony would be understandable and that's where these videotapes came from.
